blocks.text: A double point is a point through which two branches pass. Distinct real tangents give a node; coincident real tangents give a cusp.

blocks.text: Check symmetry: invariance under y→−y gives x-axis symmetry; under x→−x gives y-axis symmetry; under (x,y)→(−x,−y) gives origin symmetry; interchanging x,y tests y=x.
Find intercepts, test whether the origin lies on the curve, and use the lowest-degree terms for tangents at the origin.

For an asymptote x=a or y=b inspect the highest-power coefficients after treating the equation as a polynomial in the other variable. For an oblique line y=mx+c, substitute and equate the highest surviving coefficients.
Determine the region in which coordinates are real. Use dy/dx=0 for horizontal tangents, and check where dx/dy=0 for vertical tangents.
Use derivative signs, loops, concavity and asymptotic behaviour to join branches consistently.

items.title: Concavity and inflection
question_paragraphs: How do derivatives determine increasing/decreasing behaviour and concavity?
paragraphs: Where \(y\prime>0\), the curve increases; where \(y\prime<0\), it decreases. A zero first derivative is a stationary point, not automatically an extremum.

Where \(y^{\prime\prime}>0\), it is concave upwards; where \(y^{\prime\prime}<0\), concave downwards. Inflection requires a change of concavity. A zero second derivative alone does not establish inflection.
items.final_answer: Use derivative signs on intervals; \(y^{\prime\prime}=0\) alone is inconclusive.
